body:
Elliot Price: Heads up — final review pass on docs PR before we merge: https://github.com/redwood/redwood-docs/pull/812

Main thing I want eyes on: last-minute clarifications around tiers vs overrides (we’ve had a couple support pings on this).

Alex Martinez: Looking now. Skimming the “Batching profiles” section.

Quick gut check: are we being explicit enough that `batching_tier` only sets defaults, and any explicit knob overrides win? I want this to be unambiguous.

Wei Chen: +1. Also making sure the API examples match what Hosted actually accepts (naming / casing).

Monica Patel: I reviewed the SDK snippets earlier and I’m a little worried about the “override” example.

Right now we show:
- set `batching_tier: "cost_efficient"`
- set `max_batch_size: 64`

That’s fine, but we should say explicitly: as soon as you set `max_batch_size`, you’re no longer “pure tier defaults” — you’re in “tier + partial override”. People read “I chose cost-efficient” and assume everything is cost-efficient.

Soojin Lee: From a messaging POV: we should avoid implying that the tier is a fixed, locked profile. It’s “recommended baseline,” and overrides are supported.

Elliot Price: Yep. What wording do we want? I can change copy today.

Alex Martinez: Suggestion: add a small precedence box, something like:

1) Explicit batching knobs in the request / route config always take precedence.
2) Otherwise, the tier supplies defaults.
3) If neither is set, Redwood uses the service default (currently `standard` for supported models, otherwise legacy behavior).

Also: clarify what “unset” means.

We’ve gotten tickets where people tried to “disable max_queue_delay” by setting it to 0 and accidentally broke things.

Monica Patel: +1000 on “unset”. In the SDKs we usually treat “undefined / null” as unset, but some customers pass `0` and think it means “use tier”.

We should document:
- “omit the field” = use tier default
- “set to a value” = override

We may want to call out “0 is a real value” where relevant.

Wei Chen: I’m looking at the YAML examples. They show:

`batching_tier: fast`
`max_queue_delay_ms: 0`

We should not encourage `0` unless we truly support it as “no queueing”. Do we?

Diego Santos: For runtime: `max_queue_delay_ms: 0` is allowed but it’s basically “don’t wait” and you can tank throughput. For fast tier we actually recommend a small non-zero (like single-digit ms) to allow micro-batching without blowing p95.

So docs should not show 0 as the “fast” example.

Jordan Lee: Agree. For guardrails we also treat `0` as high-risk under load because it increases scheduling churn; more likely to hit overload protection.

Elliot Price: Got it. I’ll update examples to not use 0.

Alex Martinez: Another doc nit: we should spell the enum exactly as runtime accepts. I’ve seen `cost-efficient` vs `cost_efficient` creep.

What are we landing on?

Monica Patel: SDKs + runtime config are `cost_efficient` (snake_case). Docs should match.

Soojin Lee: Please keep it consistent everywhere. If we want a nicer display name, we can do that in Console later, but docs should be canonical.

Wei Chen: In PR right now, the heading uses “Cost-efficient” (human) and examples use `cost_efficient` (code). That’s fine, but we should add a one-liner: “Use `cost_efficient` in config.”

Alex Martinez: Re: precedence, can we add a concrete table? Something like:

- If `batching_tier=fast` and `max_batch_size` omitted → use fast default
- If `batching_tier=fast` and `max_batch_size=32` → use 32 (override)
- If `batching_tier` omitted and `max_batch_size=32` → use 32 (override)

People understand with examples.

Elliot Price: I can add a short “How precedence works” section with a table.

Monica Patel: Also add a pointer to the “effective config” / explain endpoint. Support has been asking for this, and it’s in flight.

Even if not GA, a small note like: “Console shows effective batching config; API support coming.”

Diego Santos: Runtime has `GET /v1/config/explain` behind a flag (PR 18470). It returns the computed values + the source (tier vs override). We can mention as “available in Console today; API endpoint rolling out” to avoid overpromising.

Wei Chen: +1 but careful: for Hosted API customers, they won’t have a raw endpoint unless we expose it. We should phrase it as “You can view effective config in Console” and not give an endpoint path unless it’s public.

Alex Martinez: +1. Don’t publish internal paths in docs.

Elliot Price: Ok — I’ll keep it Console-first and add a brief note: “In Console, you can inspect Effective batching settings to confirm which values come from tier defaults vs explicit overrides.”

Soojin Lee: One more: in the FAQ we say “tiers are safe-by-default.” That’s true, but if you override knobs you can break SLOs. We should add a line: “Overrides are advanced; changes may impact latency/cost and may bypass some tier guardrails.”

Jordan Lee: Yep. We do still have admission control, but you can definitely cause tail latency. A small warning box is good.

Monica Patel: I’ll also adjust the SDK snippet commentary (python + ts) in our example repos after merge. But for this PR, can we ensure the example shows overrides as optional?

Maybe structure it as:

Example A: choose a tier
Example B: choose a tier + override one knob

Right now it kind of blends them.

Elliot Price: Done. I’ll split into two sub-sections.

Alex Martinez: While you’re there, add “Streaming note” under fast tier: “fast prioritizes low queue delay and token cadence; if you’re streaming, prefer fast or standard; cost_efficient may reduce cadence.”

We keep getting this question.

Wei Chen: +1. Mention streaming explicitly in the “When to choose which tier” section.

Elliot Price: Cool. I’ll push updates in ~1h and re-request reviews.

—

Elliot Price: Pushed updates:
- Removed `max_queue_delay_ms: 0` from examples
- Added “How precedence works” table
- Clarified enum string `cost_efficient`
- Split examples: “tier only” vs “tier + override”
- Added warning box on overrides + streaming note

Can folks do a final skim? https://github.com/redwood/redwood-docs/pull/812/files

Monica Patel: Skimmed. Looks good now.

One tiny tweak: in the precedence table, can we say “request-level overrides route-level” (if that’s true)? Or are we only talking route config?

Alex Martinez: Good catch. Product intent: request overrides should win (for experimentation), but enterprise customers may disable request overrides via policy.

We should phrase it as:
- “Most specific wins: request override > route config override > tier defaults.”
- “Admins can restrict request overrides in org policy.”

Jordan Lee: Yep. Policy engine can block request overrides for certain orgs. Mentioning that is good.

Elliot Price: Added a sentence: “If your org restricts per-request overrides, the request parameters may be ignored; Console will show effective settings.”

Wei Chen: Final skim done. +1 from me. :thumbsup:

Soojin Lee: Copy reads clean. Approved.

Monica Patel: Approved. Ship it.

Alex Martinez: Approved. Thanks.

Elliot Price: Merging. Then I’ll ping examples repo folks + link this in the internal launch notes.
